news.title: Michael Nielsen took down his book on neural nets
news.summary_raw:
Article URL: https://neuralnetworksanddeeplearning.com/
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50670757
Points: 372
# Comments: 246
news.source_text:
I wrote this book between 2011 and 2015. At the time, I expected AGI systems based on neural networks to be many decades away, but to bring remarkable benefits for humanity. I also expected significant challenges, but believed it likely that, as with other technologies, those challenges would be addressed as the capabilities were developed.
My views have changed. With the extraordinarily reckless behaviour of the frontier labs, the systems have raced ahead much faster than I expected1, giving humanity far too little time to meet the challenges. Although the systems genuinely will bring — indeed, already are bringing — many wonders, they also pose a significant risk of catastrophe. The frontier labs are knowingly endangering all of humanity. I've written about why I believe this at length, most recently in “Which Future?”. Two brief thoughts are below.
I don't wish to help (even in a very small way) train people to contribute to this work, and so I've taken the book down.
Michael Nielsen
November 2026
What follows are two brief remarks: one on the nature of the threat posed by ASI, and another on the ethical justification for working on frontier AI.
The most common argument for AI existential risk, developed by Nick Bostrom and Eliezer Yudkowsky, is loss of control of the future to advanced AI systems2. I believe this concern should be understood as one instance of a more fundamental issue. That issue is whether we will discover technologies latent in nature which are easy and inexpensive to develop, catastrophic in outcome, and beyond our capacity to defend against. If such “progress” in technology were happening slowly, our social institutions might successfully develop defences. But it seems likely that ASI will cause a sudden explosion of such destructive technologies, with insufficient time to adapt.
A historical example to help prime intuition is fire. It is easy to make and extremely difficult to defend against. We have a one-cent technology, the matchstick, which requires hundreds of billions of dollars each year to defend against, as well as a whole apparatus of social institutions, technology, infrastructure and law3. AI systems will enable technologies which are far more destructive than matches. Understandably, people skeptical of catastrophic risks want these supposed threats spelled out in detail. This is intrinsically difficult, because we can't reliably anticipate future science and technology. While it is common to speculate about biothreats, I expect the worst threats will be technologies we haven't yet imagined. Nature is, after all, more imaginative than we.
Now suppose that ASI enables a 100-times speed-up in technological progress, without a matching change in the rate of social progress or social defenses. To get a sense of what the impact of such a speed-up would be, imagine that all the technological problems that occurred in the 20th century had occurred in the year 1901: the atomic bomb, the hydrogen bomb, the ICBM, chem
news.summary: Michael Nielsen has removed his book on neural networks, citing concerns that AI has advanced too rapidly and poses significant risks. He warns that frontier labs are accelerating AI development in a way that outpaces humanity’s ability to defend against catastrophic outcomes.
news.enterprise_use: Check your organization’s AI policy review schedule this week to ensure alignment with emerging risk assessments.

news.title: I am scared: Careless People – Sarah Wynn-Williams on living under a gag order
news.summary_raw:
Article URL: https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/nov/27/careless-people-author-sarah-wynn-williams-the-silence-is-mine-it-doesnt-have-to-be-yours
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50671301
Points: 144
# Comments: 66
news.source_text:
George Orwell understood that what is missing often tells you more than what is there. In Nineteen Eighty-Four, there is a slot in the wall covered by a wire grate. They call it the memory hole. When a document becomes inconvenient to the authorities – a photograph that contradicts the official line, a newspaper that remembers the wrong promise, a name that is no longer supposed to exist – you simply feed it into the slot, whereupon it is whirled away on a current of warm air to enormous hidden furnaces where it burns.
The Party doesn’t argue with the past. It removes it. Controlling the past is one of its central tools of power: “Who controls the past controls the future: who controls the present controls the past.”
Control what people are allowed to remember or what they are allowed to know, and you control what they are able to imagine. Control what they can imagine, and you have already chosen their future for them.
Knowledge matters. People need to know what actually happened. But in 2026 the language of tech has taken on a quality of manifest destiny: the men in charge have determined how it should be, as though there could be no other way, even though none of us voted for any of it.
Control of the prevailing narrative is held tacitly: the only time this authority is given voice is when it acts, decisively, to silence an alternative account. Control over narrative is becoming the real power battle in technology. The aim is not to win the argument. The aim is to leave nothing to argue with. An absence. No record. No receipt. No contestable standard of truth. No common ground of fact against which anyone could measure those in power and expose their failures. Without memory or evidence, dissent has nothing to stand on. That is why memory matters. Why evidence matters. Why books matter.
You don’t need a Ministry of Truth to make a memory hole. An employment contract will do. An NDA will do. A court order will do. A legal bill – large enough, frightening enough, open-ended enough – will do very nicely. The modern memory hole does not smell of smoke. It smells of printer toner, fresh paper and billable hours.
In libel, truth is a defence. Under an NDA, truth is the offence.
The agreement is signed at the moment of maximum vulnerability, still reeling from an “incident” while the mortgage looms and the cardboard box of family photos sits in the front seat of the car. It is signed by the gig worker, the intern, the content moderator, the production assistant, the junior publicist, the stylist. There really is no better way to knock the whistle from someone’s lips. In a justice system based broadly on the principle that sunlight is the best disinfectant, NDAs grip the elbow of truth and stay it. This is a private form of censorship, enforced by private arbitration and the public courts.

news.summary: The article discusses how modern forms of censorship—via NDAs, employment contracts, and court orders—create a ‘memory hole’ that erases inconvenient information, echoing Orwellian themes. It highlights the erosion of public record and truth in tech, stressing the need for evidence to counter power.

news.title: 9/UX: a Macintosh-inspired desktop for 9front
news.summary_raw:
Article URL: https://progrium.github.io/9ux/
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50672008
Points: 113
# Comments: 26
news.source_text:
9/UX brings the classic Mac and A/UX desktop (a spatial desktop, a global menu bar, consistent controls and dialogs, icons, and resource-driven presentation) to 9front, built the Plan 9 way: rio and libdraw draw the screen, 9P exposes every application's UI state and commands as files, namespaces define the working environment, the plumber opens documents, and ndb holds human-editable metadata.
Keep the Macintosh's direct-manipulation desktop, but make every meaningful object, action, and resource visible as a Plan 9 file.
It is not an emulator, a Macintosh ABI, or an A/UX reimplementation. Native 9front programs stay first-class, and existing rio programs (acme, sam, rc windows, nested rio) keep working unchanged beside 9/UX apps.
The pieces:
These are real frames, not mockups. The GUI tests embed h9 with a headless screen, inject mouse and keyboard input, and drive the 9P files at the same time.
Macintosh structure, Plan 9 colour: butter title bars from rio's selection yellow, acme's cream and olive, and rio's greygreen for the desktop, so 9/UX windows and legacy rio windows sit together on one screen. Everything reads in one bit, uses a sixteen-colour palette, and is drawn in whole pixels. Every graphic is original to 9/UX; it ships no Apple resources. The mockups below are generated from the same palette and metrics files as the code.
The design document describes 9/UX and its v0.1 acceptance criteria; release.md has where each one stands, the end-to-end demo, and the open issues. Every interface between components is a file protocol in docs/protocols, and the visual design covers the palette, fonts, metrics, chrome, icons and cursors.
The source is on GitHub, under the MIT license. Development runs on h9, which runs 9front's own compilers, mk and rio directly from the host shell, without booting a VM. scripts/h9.sh clones and builds the pinned h9 on its first run:
git clone https://github.com/progrium/9ux cd 9ux scripts/h9.sh --rc 'mk' scripts/h9.sh --gfx rio/7.out -u scripts/test.sh
Use rio/6.out on amd64. development.md and testing.md have the details.
9/UX is at v0.1 and under active development. Interfaces and behaviour change without notice.
Please report bugs and send questions through GitHub issues.
The 9/UX mark in the menu bar is a pixel-art Glenda by Dan Fessler. Glenda, the Plan 9 bunny, was created by Renée French.
news.summary: 9/UX introduces a Macintosh-inspired desktop environment for the 9front operating system, leveraging Plan 9’s file‑based UI architecture to expose desktop elements as 9P files. The release, currently at v0.1, offers native 9front applications alongside legacy rio programs without emulation, and is available under an MIT license on GitHub.
news.enterprise_use: Check your GitHub for the 9/UX repository to experiment with the new desktop UI in a controlled environment. While not directly impacting your existing stack, it could inspire UI design ideas for internal tools.
